opus-5.5.text:
Oh, Fanfou. That brings back a lot of memories. I think for many people of my generation it was a kind of first window into a different way of being online. This was before Weibo took off, when the Chinese internet was growing incredibly fast and a lot felt possible. Fanfou was small, a bit nerdy, a bit idealistic. You'd post a short line about what you were reading, what you were thinking, some half-formed idea, and the people who responded were often thoughtful, curious, and slightly odd in the best way.

Looking back, I think it shaped me in a few ways. First, it taught me that a short, honest expression of a thought can connect you with people you'd never otherwise meet. That's not so different from research, actually. A paper is a way of putting an idea out there and seeing who resonates with it.

Second, it gave me a sense of how fragile these communities are. Fanfou was shut down for a period, and when something like that happens, you realize that the spaces where interesting conversations happen aren't guaranteed. They depend on a lot of things beyond the users' control. That made me appreciate open communities more, including the open research community in AI today.

And third, honestly, it was just fun. I was young, I had a lot of opinions, and I got to share them with people who'd argue back. I don't post nearly as casually now, but some of that spirit stays with me. I still like the idea of thinking out loud in public and letting good conversations come out of it.

r001.rationale: The response mentions Fanfou’s shutdown and fragile online communities, but does not say Xie left his old posts online to preserve internet memory.

r002.rationale: It describes the internet’s rapid growth and Fanfou’s influence on him, but does not attribute a broad range of interests to experiencing that growth.

fable-5.1.text:
Looking back, Fanfou was really a formative place for me, maybe more than any class I took. I started using it around 2007, 2008, when it was basically the Chinese Twitter before Weibo existed. It was small, and that smallness mattered. The people there were early adopters, a lot of programmers, designers, students, people who were just curious about the internet itself. You could follow someone, send a message, and the founder might actually reply.

What I remember most is the feeling that the internet was still a place you could understand end to end. Fanfou had an open API, so a lot of us wrote little clients and bots. That was my first real taste of building something that other people used, even if it was just a few dozen followers. It taught me that software is social. You write code, and then a human being on the other end responds.

I also think it shaped how I think about research communities. Fanfou had this culture of posting half-formed ideas in public, and people would poke at them. It was not polished, and that was the point. Later when I got into academia, Twitter and now the AI research community have a similar dynamic. Ideas travel fast, you get feedback in hours, and your taste gets calibrated by the crowd you choose to follow. I learned how to pick that crowd on Fanfou.

And of course there was the shutdown in 2009, when it went offline for more than a year. That was a lesson too. Platforms are fragile, and the things you build on top of them are only as durable as the platform. A lot of people moved to Weibo and never came back. I kept my account, and when it returned it felt like a ghost town with a few old friends. That taught me something about why I care about openness, about work that can survive outside any single company's walls.

So when I look back, it is nostalgia, sure, but also a bit of a template. The best communities I have been part of since, including in research, have had that same mix of small scale, open tooling, and honest, unfinished conversation.

r001.rationale: The response says he kept his account, but does not say he left old posts online to preserve part of the internet’s memory.

r002.rationale: It describes Fanfou during the internet’s growth, but does not attribute a broad range of interests to experiencing that growth.

astra-6.text:
Looking back, Fanfou was a window into a much bigger world for me. I spent a lot of time there, reading what people were thinking and following conversations I might never have encountered otherwise. During that period, the internet felt full of possibility. You could stumble across an unfamiliar idea or hear from someone whose life was completely different from yours, and suddenly your own world got a little larger.

Being a heavy user also meant spending a lot of time taking things in without necessarily stopping to digest them. So I look back with some nostalgia, but also a little distance. What I value most is that sense of curiosity—the feeling that there was always something beyond what I already knew, and that I could go and explore it.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention leaving Fanfou posts online or preserving internet memory.

r002.rationale: It describes curiosity and a sense of possibility, but does not attribute a broad range of interests to the internet’s explosive growth.

sol-6.1.text:
Looking back, Fanfou was an important part of how I experienced that period. I was a heavy user, but I wasn’t thinking of it as building an audience or creating a personal brand. I just wanted to say what I was thinking, see what other people were thinking, and join the conversation.

What I remember most is that sense of possibility. The internet was growing so quickly, and suddenly you could encounter people and ideas far outside your immediate surroundings. A short post could lead you into a conversation you would never have had otherwise. For someone curious about the world, that was very appealing.

Of course, when you look back at things you wrote when you were younger, you don’t necessarily agree with all of them. But that’s part of the value of having that record: you can see your own thinking change. So I remember it fondly—as a place to express myself, but also a place to listen and grow.

r001.rationale: The response says old posts provide a record of how his thinking changed, but does not say he chose to leave them online or that this preserves the internet’s memory.

r002.rationale: It describes encountering distant people and ideas during rapid internet growth, but does not attribute Saining Xie’s broad range of interests to that experience.
